subject: physics_2
question_text: Why are household appliances connected in parallel?

verification.note: The mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. For this Paper-II bank the two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers. NOTE: the book prints this question TWICE in this chapter — as VSAQ 6 (this card) and again as VSAQ 20, with different answer wordings (VSAQ 6: same voltage + a fused appliance does not stop the rest; VSAQ 20: each device switches on and off independently). Both cards are authored because both are printed. Physics hand-checked: in parallel each appliance sits directly across the supply, so each gets the full supply voltage and an open branch does not break the others' circuits.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Same voltage across each
lines: In a parallel connection, each appliance is
So every appliance gets the full supply
voltage and works at its rated power.
steps.margin_note: First mark. Each appliance gets the SAME, full supply voltage.
steps.why: Appliances are designed for the supply voltage. In series the voltage would divide between them, so none would receive the voltage it is built for.
common_mistakes: Saying the current is the same through each appliance. In parallel the VOLTAGE is the same; the currents differ.
Saying parallel connection saves power. The reason is the voltage, not saving power.

recall.must_convey: That in parallel every appliance gets the full supply voltage, which is the voltage it is designed for.
accept: each appliance gets the full supply voltage
each works at its rated power
reject: if one fuses the others keep working

steps.memory_tip: Parallel shares the voltage equally: every branch sees the full supply.

steps.label: Each works independently
steps.mark_note: One failing does not stop the rest
lines: Each appliance has its own separate path.
If one appliance is fused, the circuits of
the remaining appliances are not broken,

lines.text: Full voltage to each + independent paths

steps.margin_note: Second mark. A fused appliance breaks only its own branch.
steps.why: In series one break stops the whole line, because there is only one path. Parallel branches are separate paths, so a break in one leaves the others complete.
common_mistakes: Saying the other appliances get more voltage when one fuses. Each branch still sees the same supply voltage.

recall.must_convey: That each appliance has its own path, so one fused appliance does not stop the others.
accept: if one fuses the others keep working
each has its own separate path
one break does not stop the rest
reject: each appliance gets the full supply voltage

steps.memory_tip: Two reasons, one word each: voltage (full) and paths (separate).

insider_note: Two distinct reasons earn the two marks — same full voltage, and independent branches. One reason written twice earns one.
